For a person to receive a shock, there must be 2 conditions met:

- There is a source of potential difference (electrical fault or leakage current)
- The person becomes part of a low resistance, complete electrical circuit connected to the source

**Danger Thresholds**

Macroshock: current through two points of body. Safe \<10mA, VF 100mA\
Microshock: enters body through internal device close to heart. Safe \<10μA, VF 100μA

Determinants of Severity:

- Frequency 60Hz most dangerous 
- ↑ Current 
- ↑ Density 
- ↑ Duration 
- Path (i.e. through Heart)

The risk is reduced by requiring special safety criteria for 

- Electrical supply design of the OR
- Biomedical equipment design 

**Electrical Supply Safety Features **

Operating theatres is classified as a Cardiac Protected Treatment Area 

This requires the implementation of 3 safety features 

- Residual current device (RCD) and/or
- Line isolation monitor (LIM) and
- Equipotential earthing system (EES)  

**RCD** 

- Monitors the current difference between active and neutral lines 
- if current leak occurs (greater the 10mA) through person or equipment grounding →  RCD tripped and interrupt power supply 

**Line Isolation Supply with Line Isolation Monitor**

- Uses a transformer inductor so 2 circuits not physically connected and supply 'floating' and isolated from earth
- Separate Earthing line to equipment casing 

Line isolation monitor tests circuit resistance to earth in lines active and neutral lines 

**1 Fault condition**

- Fault if impedance difference between lines
- Alarm will sound 
- Power Not interrupted 

If 2 Fault condition where secondary circuit to earth occurs then power not shut off  → results in shock

Advantage: Power supply not interrupted to essential equipment in single fault condition 

Disadvantage: not shock protection in 2 fault situations  

**Equipotential Earthing System (EES) **

Only method that protects from micro shock

- Ultra-low resistance earth cables are attached to electrical devices and the patients be
- These cables are then attached to special wall earth connector
- This ensures all equipment is referenced to a common ground, minimising the risk of leakage currents between devices and the patient

**Equipment Design **

Classified on designs to limit shock

**Class I**

- Equipment that has an earth wire connected to its outer metal casing
- This protects against shock in case a fault causes the active wire to contact the outer 
  case

**Class II** 

- Double insulated equipment
- Has a plastic outer case in addition to the normal internal insulation
- An earth wire is not required as the outer casing is non-conductive 

**Class III**

- Extra low voltage (\< 40V) or battery powered equipment
- Doesn't require an earth wire, even if it has a metal case because the voltage is low so that the risk of macroshock is negligible 

**Electrically Safe Areas**

**B Areas**: Protection against macroshock

- Residual Current Devices
- Line Isolation Supply

**BF areas**: Cardiac (microshock) protection

- Equipotential Earthing
- All devices, and the patient, are earthed to each other by thick copper (i.e. low-resistance), such that any potential difference between devices will be equalised via the path of least resistance (the wire, not the patient).

**Z areas**: No particular protections
